name: Miller's Law
aliases: The magical number seven, plus or minus two
statement: Working memory holds about seven items, plus or minus two.
statementAccent: seven items, plus or minus two
meaning: The number of distinct things an average person can keep in immediate memory at once is small and roughly fixed — about five to nine. The way to hold more is to group information into meaningful units, or 'chunks': the limit is on the number of chunks, not the number of raw letters or digits inside them.
mechanism: A chunk is the largest meaningful unit a person recognises, so what counts as one chunk depends on their knowledge — a familiar word is a single chunk for a native speaker but many for a stranger to the language. Recoding raw items into fewer, richer chunks raises effective capacity. Miller also noticed that people can reliably tell apart only a few levels of a single dimension like pitch or brightness — about two to three bits — and remarked on the numerical coincidence with memory span, but concluded the two limits were probably separate, not one shared mechanism.

examples.text: A ten-digit number is far easier to recall grouped as 555-867-5309 — three chunks — than as ten loose digits. The classic demonstration of recoding raw items into fewer meaningful units.

Confusingly, George Miller has two 'laws'. This one is about memory capacity. The other, from communication, holds that to understand someone you must first assume what they say is true and imagine what it could be true of — a cousin of the principle of charity, and a completely separate idea.

The rule is often bent to argue menus should have no more than seven items. That is a misapplication: menus rely on recognition, not recall — the options are visible on screen — so memory span does not constrain them, and broad, shallow menus often beat artificially short ones.

variants.name: Cowan's magical number four
variants.text: The modern revision: Nelson Cowan (2001) argued that once chunking and rehearsal are controlled, the pure capacity of the focus of attention is closer to four chunks in young adults — the widely accepted current estimate.

variants.name: Chunking
variants.text: The mechanism that lets the limit be worked around: grouping raw information into meaningful units, so a fixed number of chunks carries more content.

whyItMatters: It planted the idea that human short-term memory is small, capacity-limited, and chunk-based — one of the founding results of cognitive psychology and among the most-cited papers in the field. Even after the specific number was revised down, the underlying picture endures and shapes how information is designed to be remembered.

working.lead: Design for chunks, not raw items
working.text: group information into meaningful units so people carry more within a fixed number of slots — the practical payoff of the whole idea.

working.lead: Use four, not seven, as the honest estimate
working.text: for uncushioned capacity without rehearsal, Cowan's ~4 is the better modern figure; treat 7±2 as directionally right, not exact.

working.lead: Don't apply it to visible choices
working.text: recognition tasks — menus, lists on screen — are not limited by memory span, so the '7 items' rule does not follow from Miller's work.

limits: The specific 'seven' has been superseded: Nelson Cowan's 2001 reconsideration put uncushioned capacity nearer four chunks (fewer in children and older adults). Miller's number blended two different tasks — absolute judgement of one-dimensional stimuli and memory span — which he himself flagged as possibly coincidental and which later work treats as separate limits. Span also varies by material, roughly seven for digits, six for letters, five for words, and some accounts argue the real constraint is time or rehearsal rather than a fixed item count. The popular 'seven menu items' rule is a genuine misapplication.
misreadings: It is not a precise, universal constant, and it does not say a person can comprehend only seven things or that interfaces should cap options at seven. Miller's 'magical' was ironic — he opened by complaining of being persecuted by an integer and insisted there was nothing magical about it. The honest modern reading is that working memory is small and chunk-based, with about four uncushioned chunks the better estimate.
origin: From George A. Miller's 1956 paper 'The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two: Some Limits on Our Capacity for Processing Information' (Psychological Review), written at Harvard. Its estimate was revised toward four chunks by Nelson Cowan's 2001 reconsideration in Behavioral and Brain Sciences.

sources.text: Miller, G.A. (1956). "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two." Psychological Review, 63(2), 81–97.
Cowan, N. (2001). "The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity." Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1), 87–114.
"Myth #23: Choices should always be limited to 7±2," UX Myths. — the recognition-versus-recall menu-design misapplication.
